 B.C. election: Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gives victory speech after projected win; NDP's Eby resigns | CBC Loaded LIVE UPDATES BRITISH COLUMBIA VOTES B.C. election: Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gives victory speech after projected win; NDP's Eby resigns
 Updated 4 minutes ago Conservative majority would be the provincial party's first since 1928 B.C. Votes 2026
 LIVE Started 3 hours ago Voters across the province go to the polls to elect their next premier and government. Join hosts Gloria Macarenko and Jason D'Souza along with Stephen Quinn, Michelle Eliot and Justin McElroy for live coverage and analysis as results come in from from across the province.
 The Latest
 The B.C. Conservatives have toppled the incumbent B.C. NDP to win a majority government, CBC News projects, the party's first in nearly a century.
 "B.C. is definitely blue," Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said in a jubilant victory speech.
 David Eby, who called an election two years early in hopes his party would win a stronger, fourth term, resigned as premier and NDP leader in his concession speech. 
 Green Party Leader Emily Lowan is projected to win her first seat in the legislature, while the leaders of OneBC and CentreBC are both projected to lose their seats.
 CBC News has live election night coverage on this page, as well as in the video above. For riding-by-riding results, tap here .

 43 minutes ago Historic win projected for the B.C. Conservative Party
 Justin McElroy Doerkson arrives for his victory speech on election night. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press) All election nights are historic — but this projected Conservative Party victory will be talked about a little bit more than most campaigns.
 Five weeks ago, Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as their leader. The party was in disarray. Many MLAs elected under their banner had fled to CentreBC. Lorne Doerkson was vacationing in Africa. 
 Today, Doerkson is the incoming premier. The Conservative Party has formed government for the first time in this province since 1928. The New Democrats could have their smallest caucus since the 2001 election, when they were reduced to just two seats. 
 The decision by the Conservatives to quickly coalesce around Doerkson, pivot their message to the economy, and install former B.C. Liberal organizers as their campaign managers will be studied and debated for years. 
 But it’s likely the bigger focus will be on Eby’s decision to follow through with a snap election even after Findlay’s resignation.
 While many people will say many things about the choice, it brings to mind the adage often attributed to Napoleon Bonaparte: "Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake."
 What a difference five weeks makes.

 4 minutes ago Doerkson outlines future of Conservative majority
 Lauren Vanderdeen Doerkson during tonight's speech. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press) Doerkson is making promises in his victory speech. He says Vancouver will host a business summit next year that will be the "envy of the world."
 "We will welcome capital back to our province," Doerkson says.
 He promises to double natural gas production by 2032 and triple it by 2035. He wants to cut red tape "like never before."
 "We will be the catalyst, I promise you that. But you are the engine."
 And another pledge: a $1,000 tax cut and no new taxes. 
 Copy the link to this update: Doerkson outlines future of Conservative majority 
 17 minutes ago Doerkson full of joy in victory speech
 Lauren Vanderdeen Doerkson arrives for his victory speech. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press) Lorne Doerkson has walked out to Fleetwood Mac's Don't Stop for his victory speech. He entered Conservative headquarters to sparklers, celebrations and jubilant hugs.
 "B.C. is definitely blue," yells Doerkson.
 He's thanking candidates, supporters and all voters. Doerkson, who has been repeatedly described as mild-mannered during this campaign, is full of energy and excitement. This is not a mild-mannered speech.
 "I have had a lot of coffee in the last couple of weeks. Frankly, I've had quite a bit tonight," he said. 
 He promised he will work as hard as the volunteers worked on the campaign — and he's promising to "supercharge British Columbia."
 He says it won't happen on one street or one city, but all over.
 "A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps a port busy in Delta. It's one economy and it runs through every town on our map in British Columbia."

 27 minutes ago Emily Lowan projected to win 1st seat as MLA
 Lauren Vanderdeen Lowan, right, hugs a friend tonight. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press) CBC News is projecting B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan will be the next MLA for Saanich North and the Islands.
 Elected as party leader last year, Lowan did not have a seat in the legislature. In her first campaign for public office, she ran in the riding formerly held by the Greens' Rob Botterell.
 Lowan, 26, has previously worked as a climate activist and a policy researcher.

 38 minutes ago Eby resigns as premier, B.C. NDP leader as he concedes election
 Tara Carman FULL SPEECH: David Eby concedes and resigns as NDP leader
 20 minutes ago | Duration closed caption 6:11 David Eby, speaking to party supporters, has conceded the election and resigned as NDP leader. He says he spoke to the Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson and wished him the best as the incoming premier of British Columbia.
 Eby is giving his concession speech at a downtown Vancouver hotel. He says he congratulated Doerkson on winning a majority government.
 “The people of British Columbia have asked us to be the Official Opposition," Eby said.
 “It breaks my heart and I accept full responsibility for that outcome.”
 He then offered his resignation as premier and B.C. NDP leader. Eby he’s looking forward to spending more time with his wife and three young children.
 “My family has paid a very significant cost for this work," he said.
 He ended his speech by telling his wife, Dr. Cailey Lynch, that he loves her and saying, “let’s go home."

 59 minutes ago Sturko ousted in Surrey-Cloverdale, CBC News projects
 Lauren Vanderdeen Sturko is pictured before the campaign. (Ben Nelms/CBC) Elenore Sturko, leader of CentreBC, has lost her seat in Surrey-Cloverdale, CBC News projects.
 Sturko was first elected in 2022 as a B.C. Liberal, which later became B.C. United. She made headlines as one of the first defectors to the B.C. Conservatives and was re-elected in 2024. 
 In September 2025, former party leader John Rustad kicked Sturko out of the Conservative caucus . She then sat as an Independent in the legislature.
 Last month, Sturko was one of several former Conservative MLAs who joined CentreBC under the leadership of Peter Milobar. While others returned to the Conservatives when Kerry-Lynne Findlay stepped down as leader, Sturko stayed with CentreBC and became its leader.
 Copy the link to this update: Sturko ousted in Surrey-Cloverdale, CBC News projects 
 1 hour ago Dallas Brodie projected to lose seat
 Lauren Vanderdeen OneBC leader Dallas brodie says getting just one candidate elected 'would be phenomenal'
 1 hour ago | Duration closed caption 2:34 OneBC leader tells the CBC's Tanya Fletcher her party is the 'voice of true conservatism' in B.C. and that getting just one candidate across the line would be phenomenal. Her party currently has no projected MLAs elected.
 OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie is projected to lose her seat in Vancouver-Quilchena .
 Brodie was elected in 2024 with the B.C. Conservatives, but  then-leader John Rustad kicked out of the caucus five months after the election for her comments about  residential school survivors. 
 Brodie formed OneBC as a party for social conservatives with Tara Armstrong, an MLA who resigned from the Conservatives in solidarity with Brodie. The two split up in late 2025 .
 This past summer, Brodie survived a recall campaign that failed to get even a quarter of the number of signatures needed to remove her from office.
 Copy the link to this update: Dallas Brodie projected to lose seat 
 1 hour ago Conservative HQ vibrating with excitement
 Tarnjit Parmar Supporters hug at the Conservative watch party in Vancouver after seeing new results. (Chris Helgren/Reuters) Hundreds of people exploded into cheers as CBC News projected a majority government for the B.C. Conservatives. 
 The Rocky Mountaineer Station is vibrating with energy as party supporters celebrate. 
 The win is a historic one as the Conservative Party of B.C. will form government for the first time in 98 years. Leader Lorne Doerkson is not at the viewing party, but will make a speech to supporters later tonight.
 Copy the link to this update: Conservative HQ vibrating with excitement 
 1 hour ago BREAKING: B.C. Conservatives win majority government, CBC News projects
 Rhianna Schmunk CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government
 60 minutes ago | Duration closed caption 1:59 CBC News is projecting the B.C. Conservative Party, led by the 'accidental leader' Lorne Doerkson, will win the majority of seats in the province's legislature.
 The B.C. Conservatives have toppled the incumbent B.C. NDP to win a majority government, CBC News projects, the party's first in nearly a century.
 The result means voters firmly embraced newcomer leader Lorne Doerkson’s calls for change and sent the Conservative party to lead in the legislature for the first time in 98 years.
 The triumph for Doerkson, 58, was a powerful rejection of the current government and a seismic victory for an embattled party that sought to appeal to disillusioned voters after nearly a decade of NDP rule. The result also marked a stunning comeback for a party that appeared to not stand a chance at forming government just months ago, having weathered intense political turmoil for months.
 Copy the link to this update: BREAKING: B.C. Conservatives win majority government, CBC News projects 
 1 hour ago Conservative dominance holding
 Justin McElroy More than 250,000 votes are in at this point, and it’s hard to imagine a better start for the B.C. Conservative Party.
 Some of the seats they’re currently leading in are due to small vote sizes: it’s extremely unlikely they will end up winning three seats in East Vancouver where they’re currently ahead, for example.
 But they’re sweeping Richmond and Surrey, and leading in all the swing ridings that they targeted as potential pickups.
 B.C. is used to long election nights. This one might end up being fairly short.
